subcategory: Texas blackland prairie native annual wildflower

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto bare ground alongside other winter annual wildflowers; this diminutive phlox needs open, unmulched soil to germinate and will go dormant again after setting seed in late spring.

directions: Pointed phlox is a low, slender winter annual native to the sandy and clay prairies of Texas, Oklahoma, and Louisiana, where it often blooms alongside bluebonnets and other spring ephemerals on the Blackland Prairie's darker soils. Direct sow seed onto bare ground in fall so it can germinate with the season's first cool rains, form a low rosette through winter, and send up five-petaled flowers in shades of white, pink, or purple from late winter into late spring. It thrives in lean, well-drained soil in full sun and needs no supplemental care once established, reseeding readily if seed heads are left to mature and shatter. Keep plantings in open, undisturbed ground, since taller grasses and mulch can quickly crowd out this diminutive annual.

subcategory: Texas blackland prairie native annual/biennial wildflower

planting.note: Direct sow in spring in full sun on lean to average, well-drained soil, including heavy clay; established plants bloom from late summer into fall and self-sow freely in open ground.

directions: Spanish gold is a coarse, resinous-leaved annual-to-short-lived-perennial native to the Great Plains from Iowa and Nebraska south through Oklahoma into the clay prairies of North and Central Texas, including the Blackland belt. Branching, pale green stems lined with spiny-toothed, clasping leaves rise to several feet and open into bright yellow, daisy-like flower heads coated in a sticky resin from late summer into fall, a late-season nectar source when much of the prairie has gone dormant. It tolerates drought and roadside disturbance without complaint once established, growing equally well in lean sand or heavy clay. Best suited to informal meadow or prairie-restoration plantings rather than tidy borders, since it self-sows readily and has a rangy, open habit.

subcategory: Texas blackland prairie native annual legume

planting.note: Direct sow scarified seed in fall onto bare, well-drained soil; this climbing winter annual legume scrambles over neighboring prairie plants and blooms from April into June.

directions: Louisiana vetch is a slender, tendril-climbing winter annual legume native throughout the southern prairies and open woodlands of Texas, where its nitrogen-fixing roots help enrich the heavy clay soils of the Blackland belt. Sow seed in fall onto open ground so it can germinate with autumn rains, scramble low over neighboring grasses and forbs through winter, and open small lavender-blue pea flowers from April into June. It asks for nothing beyond full sun and average to lean soil, needs no irrigation once established, and offers valuable browse and cover for wildlife along with a mild soil-building effect in a native meadow planting. Allow seed pods to ripen and shatter for reliable self-sowing in following years.

subcategory: Texas blackland prairie native warm-season bunchgrass

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification into well-drained sandy or clay soil in full sun; clumps establish slowly but are long-lived once rooted in.

directions: Silveus' dropseed is a tall, clump-forming perennial bunchgrass restricted to a narrow native range in eastern Texas and western Louisiana, where it is a signature species of the globally rare blackland prairie remnants found at the convergence of the Blackland Prairie, Post Oak Savannah, and Pineywoods. Fibrous-rooted clumps send up slender flowering culms to about four feet, opening airy, green-and-purple-tinged panicles from midsummer through fall. Plants establish slowly from seed but persist for decades once rooted in, needing no fertilizer or supplemental irrigation beyond normal rainfall in their native range. Because true blackland prairie habitat is so reduced, this species remains a valuable but still underused choice for serious prairie-restoration plantings.

subcategory: Texas blackland prairie native warm-season bunchgrass

planting.note: Direct sow into a well-prepared, weed-free seedbed in spring after soil has warmed; seedling vigor is low, so keep competing weeds down until the bunchgrass is established.

directions: Brownseed paspalum is a warm-season perennial bunchgrass native across the Blackland Prairie, Post Oak Savannah, and Gulf Prairie regions of Texas, where it grows in moist sandy loam to clay soils in open prairie and at woodland margins. Upright, leafy clumps two to three feet tall send up narrow seed spikes from late spring through fall, adding seasonal forage and ground cover value to restoration and pasture plantings. Seedlings are slow to establish, so sow into a clean, weed-free bed in spring and keep competition down until the grass's root system develops; growth is vigorous once established. Mature stands tolerate periodic mowing or light grazing and need no irrigation beyond normal rainfall within their native range.
